warmup.q: A nightly Airflow task runs INSERT INTO daily_totals SELECT ... WHERE day = '{{ ds }}'. One night its worker is killed after the INSERT committed but before Airflow heard back. Airflow retries the task, and the retry succeeds. What does daily_totals hold for that day?
options: One row: Airflow undoes a failed attempt before it retries
Two rows: the day is counted twice
No rows: the failed attempt's transaction was rolled back
One row: the database refuses the duplicate
warmup.why: The first INSERT had committed before the worker died, so its row stays. Airflow only knows the attempt didn't report success; it can't undo work a task did in another system, and it runs the task again. Without a unique constraint the database accepts the second row. With one, the retry fails instead, which is still not a correct pipeline. The fix is a write that replaces the day, so running twice leaves what running once does.

sections.h: Three schedulers decide where, how and when
sections.html:
The nightly settlement pipeline is three jobs. Job 1 imports the acquirer's settlement file. Job 2 is a Spark job that builds settlement lines from it. Job 3 publishes the report finance reads at 08:00.

Version 1 is cron: job 1 at 00:30, job 2 at 02:00, job 3 at 04:00, with the gaps guessed from how long each job usually takes. It works most nights. On the nights the acquirer's file lands two hours late, job 2 starts at 02:00 anyway and builds the report from a half-imported day; in the Try it that happens on 2 of 30 nights, and nothing fails, so nobody notices. Cron also doesn't retry a job that died, doesn't stop two runs of the same job from overlapping, and keeps no record of which day each run was for.

Version 2 states the dependencies and lets a program start each job when the jobs it needs have finished. The jobs and their "must finish before" edges form a DAG, a directed acyclic graph. Acyclic means no job depends on itself through a chain, so there is always an order that runs every job after everything it needs: a topological order. The program that runs DAGs is a workflow orchestrator: Apache Airflow (3.4 is current), Dagster and Prefect are the common ones. Each run of a DAG is for one logical date, the day of data it processes, which is not the same as the moment it runs: the run for 6 November starts in the early hours of 7 November, or months later in a backfill.

The orchestrator is only the top of three layers that all schedule something, as the figure shows. The middle layer is the engine's own scheduler. Lesson 6 showed Spark's driver splitting a job into stages and tasks and retrying a failed task from its lineage, up to 4 attempts by default (spark.task.maxFailures); Airflow never sees those tasks. The bottom layer is the resource manager, which decides which machine runs each process and with how much CPU and memory: YARN on Hadoop clusters, Kubernetes almost everywhere else. On Kubernetes the Spark driver runs in a pod and asks the Kubernetes API for executor pods (Spark 4.3's documentation lists Kubernetes 1.34 or newer), and the kubelet on each node runs them in cgroups, the Operating systems track's containers lesson.

Resource managers share a cluster between jobs that each want more than their share. Say 160 cores and two jobs that each ask for 100. The scheduler can give each 80, run one and queue the other, or take cores away from a low-priority job that is already running, which kills its tasks. Batch work is the usual victim, because it can be redone: it runs on cheap capacity that the cloud provider can reclaim at short notice, and DDIA cites Google's Borg paper for the observation that tasks are killed by preemption more often than by hardware faults. So every layer retries, and the rest of this lesson is about making retries safe.

try.title: Cron's guess against a DAG's dependency
steps: Run CronVsDagDemo. It simulates 30 nights. The acquirer's file usually lands around 00:30 and sometimes hours late, the import takes 40 to 80 minutes, and the report starts either at 02:00 (cron) or when the import finishes (a DAG).
Before reading: on how many nights will the cron report be wrong, and will any of its runs fail?
Is the DAG's report always later than cron's? Look at the median.

code.title: CronVsDagDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l13.demo import kotlin.random.Random /** * Thirty nights of a two-job pipeline. Job 1 imports the acquirer's settlement file, which usually * lands at about 00:30 but some nights is hours late. Job 2 builds the settlement report from it. * With cron, job 2 starts at 02:00 every night, a guess that "job 1 is surely done by then". With * a DAG, job 2 starts when job 1 finishes. */ fun main() { val rnd = Random(2026) fun clock(m: Int) = "%02d:%02d".format(m / 60, m % 60) var wrong = 0 val cronReady = mutableListOf<Int>() val dagReady = mutableListOf<Int>() println("night file lands import done cron report (02:00) DAG report") for (night in 1..30) { val late = rnd.nextDouble() < 0.1 val lands = 30 + if (late) 60 + rnd.nextInt(120) else rnd.nextInt(15) val imported = lands + 40 + rnd.nextInt(40) // the import takes 40 to 80 minutes val cronOk = imported <= 120 if (!cronOk) wrong++ cronReady += 120 + 10 dagReady += imported + 10 // the report itself takes 10 minutes if (!cronOk || night <= 3) { println("%5d %10s %11s %-25s %s".format(night, clock(lands), clock(imported), if (cronOk) "${clock(130)}, right" else "${clock(130)}, read a partial day", "${clock(imported + 10)}, right")) } } println("(nights 4 to 30 not shown unless cron got them wrong)") println("cron: $wrong of 30 reports built from a partial import; every report ready at ${clock(130)}") println("DAG: 0 of 30 wrong; reports ready at a median ${clock(dagReady.sorted()[15])}, the latest at ${clock(dagReady.max())}") }

try.expect:
night  file lands  import done  cron report (02:00)        DAG report
    1       00:33        01:34  02:10, right               01:44, right
    2       00:41        01:54  02:10, right               02:04, right
    3       00:40        01:35  02:10, right               01:45, right
    4       02:09        03:01  02:10, read a partial day  03:11, right
   25       02:41        03:23  02:10, read a partial day  03:33, right
(nights 4 to 30 not shown unless cron got them wrong)
cron: 2 of 30 reports built from a partial import; every report ready at 02:10
DAG:  0 of 30 wrong; reports ready at a median 01:52, the latest at 03:33

On 28 nights the guess of 02:00 was safe, and on two nights the file landed after 02:00, so the cron report read a day that was still being imported. Neither run failed, which is the dangerous part. The DAG started the report when the import finished: it was never wrong, it was usually earlier than cron (a median of 01:52), and on the two late nights it was later, because there was nothing correct to report before then. The run is deterministic, so you get the same nights.

sections.h: A retry is safe only if running twice equals running once
sections.html:
Every layer retries, so every task runs more than once sooner or later. Lesson 3 showed when re-running is harmless: MapReduce reran a lost task from the same immutable input, and the task's output became visible only through an atomic rename, so a second attempt could never leave two copies. Inside one engine, those rules hold by design.

The orchestrator's tasks break them, because they write to other systems: a warehouse table, a database, an API. And the orchestrator can't see inside them. It knows that an attempt started and that it either reported success or didn't. The case that does the damage is a task that did its writes and then died before reporting success: the worker was preempted, the pod ran out of memory during clean-up, the network dropped the reply. The orchestrator sees a failed attempt and runs it again. The stepper follows one such night.

A task that is safe to retry is idempotent: running it twice leaves the same result as running it once. Three rules get you there.

  1. Read a fixed input: the partition for the run's logical date. Never "the latest data" or now(), because a retry tomorrow, or a backfill next month, would read something else.
  2. Write by replacing, never by adding: overwrite the day's partition (INSERT OVERWRITE ... PARTITION), delete and insert the day in one transaction, MERGE on a key, or make one table-format commit that replaces the day (lessons 11 and 12). Appending with INSERT INTO adds a second copy on every retry.
  3. Make the output appear in one step, so a crash leaves the old result or the new one, never half of each.

Airflow's best-practices guide says the same in its own words: treat a task like a database transaction that never leaves partial results, use upserts instead of inserts, and read the partition for data_interval_start instead of the latest data. Prefect 3 makes "at most once" part of the API: a transaction with a key writes a record when it commits, and a rerun with the same key finds the record and skips the work.

In the Try it, one night's load task crashes right after writing its total. With INSERT INTO, the retry writes a second row and the report shows 11,949,314 cents for a day whose payments add up to 5,974,657. With a partition overwrite, the retry replaces the row and the report is right. Over 90 nights where a crash like that hits a fifth of the loads, the appending pipeline ends up 28% too high, and a retry policy alone made it worse.

try.title: Crash a load after its write, then retry
steps: Run RetryDemo. It runs one night with a load that crashes after writing and is retried, once with an appending load and once with an overwriting load, then 90 nights where such crashes hit at random.
Predict the report for each load before reading the output.
Some nights crashed twice. What does the appending table hold for such a night?

code.title: RetryDemo.kt (the pipeline is in Model.kt)
code.html: package sfz.batch.l13.demo import java.time.LocalDate import kotlin.random.Random /** * One night where the load task's worker dies right after it wrote its result, run with an * appending load and with an overwriting load. Then 90 nights with random crashes of that kind. */ fun main() { val day = LocalDate.of(2026, 11, 6) for ((name, load) in listOf("append (INSERT INTO)" to append, "overwrite the partition" to overwrite)) { val w = Warehouse() println("load = $name") runDay(w, day, load, crashes = 1) { println(" $it") } println(" the source says %,d cents".format(payments(day).sum())) } val days = (0 until 90).map { LocalDate.of(2026, 8, 9).plusDays(it.toLong()) } val rnd = Random(7) val crashes = days.associateWith { var n = 0; while (n < 2 && rnd.nextDouble() < 0.2) n++; n } val truth = days.sumOf { payments(it).sum() } println("90 nights, each load crashing after its write with chance 20% (sometimes twice): ${crashes.values.count { it > 0 }} nights hit") for ((name, load) in listOf("append" to append, "overwrite" to overwrite)) { val w = Warehouse() days.forEach { runDay(w, it, load, crashes.getValue(it)) } val wrong = days.count { w.read("daily_totals", it) != listOf(payments(it).sum()) } println(" %-9s total %,15d cents, %+.1f%% against the source, %d wrong days".format(name, w.total("daily_totals"), 100.0 * (w.total("daily_totals") - truth) / truth, wrong)) } }

try.expect:
load = append (INSERT INTO)
  minute   5  extract   attempt 1: staging has 235 payments, ok
  minute  15  load      attempt 1: wrote its total, daily_totals now has 1 row(s), then the worker died
  minute  20  scheduler retries load after 5 minutes
  minute  30  load      attempt 2: wrote its total, daily_totals now has 2 row(s), ok
  minute  35  report    attempt 1: reports the day as 11,949,314 cents
  the source says 5,974,657 cents
load = overwrite the partition
  minute   5  extract   attempt 1: staging has 235 payments, ok
  minute  15  load      attempt 1: wrote its total, daily_totals now has 1 row(s), then the worker died
  minute  20  scheduler retries load after 5 minutes
  minute  30  load      attempt 2: wrote its total, daily_totals now has 1 row(s), ok
  minute  35  report    attempt 1: reports the day as 5,974,657 cents
  the source says 5,974,657 cents
90 nights, each load crashing after its write with chance 20% (sometimes twice): 21 nights hit
  append    total     720,540,797 cents, +28.0% against the source, 21 wrong days
  overwrite total     563,126,222 cents, +0.0% against the source, 0 wrong days

The two pipelines did exactly the same things in the same order; only the load's write differed. The appending load left one row per attempt, so the report doubled the day. The overwriting load replaced the day's partition on each attempt, so the retry was harmless. Over 90 nights, 21 had a crash of this kind, and the appending pipeline's total ended 28% above the source: some nights crashed twice and were counted three times. Every run reported success in the end.

sections.h: A backup copy fixes a slow machine, not a big partition
sections.html:
A stage of a batch job finishes when its slowest task finishes. One slow task, a straggler, holds back everything after it. The MapReduce paper lists real causes: a machine whose failing disk had dropped from 30 MB/s to 1 MB/s, other jobs competing for the same machine, and a bug that switched off the processor caches and made some machines more than 100 times slower.

Version 1 is to wait. With backup tasks switched off, the paper's 1 TB sort took 1,283 seconds instead of 891, 44% longer, and its last five tasks alone added about 300 seconds.

Version 2 is the backup task: near the end of a job, start a second copy of every task still running, on another machine, and take whichever copy finishes first. The paper puts the cost at a few percent more computing resources, and it removed the tail. The same paper killed 200 of 1,746 worker processes in the middle of the sort, and the job finished in 933 seconds, 5% slower than normal, because their tasks were simply rerun elsewhere.

Spark calls it speculative execution, and it is off by default (spark.speculation=false). When you turn it on, Spark checks every 100 ms, and once 90% of a stage's tasks have finished (spark.speculation.quantile), any task running more than 3 times the median task time (spark.speculation.multiplier) gets a copy on a free slot. Since Spark 3.4 it first checks that the task is really progressing slowly for its input (spark.speculation.efficiency.enabled). It's off by default for the reason of the last section: two copies of a task run at the same time. Their output must commit atomically and carry no outside effects, or a task that writes to a database or calls an API does it twice.

And speculation only fixes one kind of straggler. If the machine is slow, the copy runs on a healthy machine and wins. If the task is slow because its partition is big, the copy reads the same big partition and is just as slow. That's lesson 8's skew: one hot key sends 30% of the rows to one task, and the fix is to split the key, with AQE's skew join or salting, not to run it twice. In the Try it, one slow machine stretched a 40-second stage to 120 seconds, and speculation brought it back to 48. One skewed task stretched it to 144 seconds, and speculation launched a copy that changed nothing.

try.title: Speculate on a slow machine and on a skewed task
steps: Run SpeculationDemo. It simulates a stage of 200 tasks on 20 slots, once with one machine 30 times slower and once with one task holding 30 times the data, each without and with Spark's speculation rule.
Predict which case speculation rescues before you read the table.
Read the stage function. When does the rule start copying tasks, and which copy wins?

code.title: SpeculationDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l13.demo /** * One stage of 200 tasks on 20 task slots, on virtual time, run four ways. In the first case one * machine (two slots) has a failing disk and runs 30 times slower. In the second, one task has 30 * times the data of the others (a skewed key). Each case runs without and with speculation, using * Spark's rule: once 90% of the stage's tasks are done, a task running longer than 3 times the * median task time gets a copy on a free slot, and whichever copy finishes first wins. */ fun main() { println("%-34s %18s %18s".format("stage of 200 tasks, 20 slots", "no speculation", "speculation")) for ((name, slowSlots, bigTask) in listOf( Triple("one slow machine (2 slots, 30x)", setOf(0, 1), -1), Triple("one skewed task (30x the data)", emptySet(), 137), )) { val plain = stage(slowSlots, bigTask, speculate = false) val spec = stage(slowSlots, bigTask, speculate = true) println("%-34s %15.1f s %15.1f s (%d speculative %s)".format(name, plain.first, spec.first, spec.second, if (spec.second == 1) "copy" else "copies")) } println("a healthy stage takes %.1f s".format(stage(emptySet(), -1, speculate = false).first)) } /** Returns the stage's finish time in seconds and the number of speculative copies launched. */ private fun stage(slowSlots: Set<Int>, bigTask: Int, speculate: Boolean): Pair<Double, Int> { val tasks = 200 val slots = 20 val work = DoubleArray(tasks) { if (it == bigTask) 30.0 * 4 else 4.0 } // seconds on a healthy slot val speed = DoubleArray(slots) { if (it in slowSlots) 1.0 / 30 else 1.0 } data class Copy(val task: Int, val slot: Int, val start: Double) val running = mutableListOf<Copy>() val done = BooleanArray(tasks) val durations = mutableListOf<Double>() val busy = BooleanArray(slots) var next = 0 var copies = 0 var t = 0.0 val dt = 0.1 while (done.any { !it }) { // start pending tasks on free slots, lowest slot first for (s in 0 until slots) if (!busy[s] && next < tasks) { running += Copy(next++, s, t); busy[s] = true } // speculation check, as Spark does every 100 ms if (speculate && next == tasks && done.count { it } >= 0.9 * tasks) { val median = durations.sorted()[durations.size / 2] for (c in running.toList()) { val alreadyCopied = running.count { it.task == c.task } > 1 if (!alreadyCopied && t - c.start > 3 * median) { val free = (0 until slots).firstOrNull { !busy[it] } ?: continue running += Copy(c.task, free, t); busy[free] = true; copies++ } } } t += dt // finish copies whose work is done; the first copy of a task to finish wins, the other is killed for (c in running.toList()) { if (c !in running) continue if ((t - c.start) * speed[c.slot] >= work[c.task] - 1e-9) { done[c.task] = true durations += t - c.start for (o in running.filter { it.task == c.task }) { running.remove(o); busy[o.slot] = false } } } } return t to copies }

try.expect:
stage of 200 tasks, 20 slots           no speculation        speculation
one slow machine (2 slots, 30x)              120.0 s            48.0 s   (2 speculative copies)
one skewed task (30x the data)               144.0 s           144.0 s   (1 speculative copy)
a healthy stage takes 40.0 s

The two cases look the same from outside: a stage that should take 40 seconds takes two or three times as long because of one or two tasks. Speculation tells them apart by accident. On the slow machine, the two tasks that landed there got copies on healthy slots, which finished long before the originals: 48 seconds. The skewed task's copy had the same 30 times more data to process, so it was no faster, and the stage still took 144 seconds. Times are virtual seconds from the simulation, so they're the same on every machine.

sections.h: A backfill reruns history, so every task must be safe to rerun
sections.html:
A backfill runs a DAG for past logical dates. You need one whenever history has to be recomputed: a bug in the fee calculation was live for 90 days, a new report needs a year of data, a column was added to a table that existing rows should have too. Every day of history becomes one run.

Airflow 3 runs backfills inside the scheduler, from the UI, the REST API or the command line:

airflow backfill create --dag-id settlement \
    --from-date 2026-08-09 --to-date 2026-11-06 \
    --reprocess-behavior completed --max-active-runs 8

--reprocess-behavior says which days to run: none runs only days that have no run yet, failed adds days whose run failed, and completed reruns every day. --max-active-runs caps how many of the backfill's runs go at once, and it matters more than it looks: Airflow's documentation says the scheduler does not deprioritize backfill tasks, so a backfill without a cap competes on equal terms with tonight's scheduled runs. --run-backwards processes the newest days first.

The arithmetic is waves. A year of daily runs of 20 minutes each, 16 at a time, takes 23 waves: about 7.7 hours. Run backwards, the newest week is ready after 20 minutes, which is usually what people are waiting for. The Try it prints the table for 1, 4 and 16 runs at a time.

Whether a backfill is safe is decided by the tasks, not by the orchestrator. It is safe when every run reads only its own logical date's input and replaces its own output, because then running a day twice changes nothing and --reprocess-behavior completed is harmless. It is unsafe in three common ways. A task that appends doubles every day it reruns, as the Try it shows. A task that reads "the latest partition" or now() gets today's data in every historical run; the lab has one, and it copies today's total into all 90 backfilled days. A task with an outside effect, an email to each merchant or a call to a partner's API, repeats it for every day.

The newer orchestrators move the unit of work from tasks to data. In Airflow 3, a task can declare the assets it updates (tables or files), and another DAG can run whenever one of them changes. Dagster is built around software-defined assets: you declare each table and the function that computes it from its upstream tables, and running that function and storing the result is called materializing the asset. Give an asset daily partitions and a backfill becomes "materialize these 90 partitions", which only works if each partition is computed from its own inputs and replaced whole. Prefect 3 (3.9 is current) stays closer to plain Python: flows and tasks are functions marked @flow and @task.

try.title: Size a year's backfill, then run it twice
steps: Run BackfillDemo. It schedules 365 daily runs of 20 minutes with 1, 4 and 16 runs at a time, oldest first and backwards, then runs the whole backfill twice with each kind of load.
Before reading: how long does 16 at a time take? Work it out as waves.
Which number would your finance team care about first, the total time or the time until the newest week is ready?

code.title: BackfillDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l13.demo import java.time.LocalDate /** * A year of history backfilled with the daily-totals pipeline (20 minutes a run), with Airflow's * `--max-active-runs` at 1, 4 and 16, oldest first and with `--run-backwards`. Then the same backfill * run a second time, the way `--reprocess-behavior completed` would, with each kind of load. */ fun main() { val days = (0 until 365).map { LocalDate.of(2025, 11, 7).plusDays(it.toLong()) } fun hours(m: Long) = "%.1f h".format(m / 60.0) println("365 daily runs of 20 minutes:") for (active in listOf(1, 4, 16)) { val (end, firstWeekDone) = backfill(days, active, backwards = false) val (endB, newestWeekDone) = backfill(days, active, backwards = true) println(" max active runs %2d: done after %7s; the newest week is ready after %7s, or %7s with run backwards".format( active, hours(end), hours(firstWeekDone), hours(newestWeekDone))) check(end == endB) } for ((name, load) in listOf("append" to append, "overwrite" to overwrite)) { val w = Warehouse() repeat(2) { days.forEach { runDay(w, it, load, crashes = 0) } } val truth = days.sumOf { payments(it).sum() } println("backfill run twice, load = %-9s total is %.2f times the source".format(name, w.total("daily_totals").toDouble() / truth)) } } /** Returns when the whole backfill ends, and when the newest 7 days are all done, in minutes. */ private fun backfill(days: List<LocalDate>, active: Int, backwards: Boolean): Pair<Long, Long> { val freeAt = LongArray(active) val ends = mutableMapOf<LocalDate, Long>() for (d in if (backwards) days.reversed() else days) { val slot = freeAt.indices.minBy { freeAt[it] } freeAt[slot] += 20 ends[d] = freeAt[slot] } return ends.values.max() to days.takeLast(7).maxOf { ends.getValue(it) } }

try.expect:
365 daily runs of 20 minutes:
  max active runs  1: done after 121.7 h; the newest week is ready after 121.7 h, or   2.3 h with run backwards
  max active runs  4: done after  30.7 h; the newest week is ready after  30.7 h, or   0.7 h with run backwards
  max active runs 16: done after   7.7 h; the newest week is ready after   7.7 h, or   0.3 h with run backwards
backfill run twice, load = append    total is 2.00 times the source
backfill run twice, load = overwrite total is 1.00 times the source

The total time is waves times run time: ceil(365 / 16) = 23 waves of 20 minutes is 7.7 hours, if the cluster really has room for 16 runs at once. Oldest first, the newest week is ready only at the very end; backwards, it's ready in the first wave. Running the whole backfill a second time, which is what --reprocess-behavior completed does after a partial failure, doubled the appending pipeline's numbers and left the overwriting pipeline's exactly right.

analogy: A workflow orchestrator is a restaurant's expediter. Cooks (the engines) cook, the floor manager (the resource manager) decides which station each cook works at, and the expediter decides when each dish starts, based on what has to be ready first: the sauce before the plate, the plate before the pass. If a plate is dropped, the expediter calls it again. Calling a dish again is only safe if cooking it twice leaves one dish on the pass: a cook who adds a second steak to the same plate, instead of replacing the plate, turns every dropped plate into a double order. A backfill is the night the inspector asks the kitchen to recook last month's menu from the recipes and the delivery notes. The analogy breaks at the past: a kitchen can't recook yesterday's dinner, while a batch pipeline can recompute any day from its stored input, as long as each run reads only that day's input and replaces only that day's output.
world: You already write idempotent code for payments. A Temporal activity can run more than once, so you give the card-issuer call an idempotency key and make the ledger write an upsert keyed by payment id. Batch tasks need the same discipline at the size of a day: the settlement job for 6 November reads the 6 November partition and replaces the 6 November output, so an Airflow retry, a Temporal retry of the activity that submits the Spark job, or a backfill next quarter all leave the same numbers. Keep the outside effects (the email to the merchant, the payout file sent to the bank) in their own task, keyed by day and merchant with a record of what was sent, so rerunning the computation never repeats them.
mistake: The common mistake is turning on retries, or running a backfill, for tasks that append. retries=3 feels like reliability, so it goes into the default arguments of every DAG, and nothing looks wrong: each run ends green. But every attempt that died after its write leaves its rows behind, and the next attempt adds them again, so the tables drift upward a few nights a month, and a backfill with --reprocess-behavior completed doubles a whole quarter at once. People make the mistake because their tasks were written as scripts that run once, and INSERT INTO is the natural way to write a script. The fix is in the task, not the orchestrator: read the logical date's partition, replace the logical date's output in one commit (overwrite the partition, delete and insert in one transaction, or MERGE on a key), and move outside effects into a separate task that records what it already did. Then turn retries on.

worked.title: Turn a cron script into a DAG that is safe to retry and backfill

steps.say: Start from what runs today: a crontab line and a script that totals "yesterday" and appends the result. It reads relative to the clock and appends, so a rerun on any other day computes the wrong day, and a rerun on the same day doubles it.
steps.code: # crontab: 02:00 every night 0 2 * * * /opt/jobs/daily_totals.sh -- daily_totals.sh runs this SQL INSERT INTO daily_totals (day, total_cents) SELECT current_date - 1, sum(amount_cents) FROM payments WHERE created_at >= current_date - 1 AND created_at < current_date;

steps.say: Make the day a parameter. The orchestrator passes the run's logical date, so the run for 6 November computes 6 November whether it runs that night, after a retry, or in a backfill months later.
steps.code: -- :day is the run's logical date (Airflow's {{ ds }} or data_interval_start) SELECT :day, sum(amount_cents) FROM payments WHERE created_at >= :day AND created_at < :day + INTERVAL '1 day';

steps.say: Replace instead of append, in one transaction, so a crash leaves the old row or the new one and a rerun writes the same single row again.
steps.code: BEGIN; DELETE FROM daily_totals WHERE day = :day; INSERT INTO daily_totals (day, total_cents) SELECT :day, sum(amount_cents) FROM payments WHERE created_at >= :day AND created_at < :day + INTERVAL '1 day'; COMMIT;

steps.say: Put it in a DAG with its dependency on the import and with retries, which are now safe. The @dag and @task decorators come from Airflow 3's task SDK, airflow.sdk.
steps.code: from datetime import datetime, timedelta from airflow.sdk import dag, task @dag(schedule="@daily", start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1), catchup=False, default_args={"retries": 2, "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5)}) def daily_totals(): @task def import_settlement_file(ds=None): ... # reads the acquirer's file for day ds @task def load_totals(ds=None): ... # the DELETE + INSERT above, for day ds import_settlement_file() >> load_totals() daily_totals()

steps.say: Recompute the 90 days a bug was live: a backfill, capped so tonight's runs still get scheduled, newest first so this week's numbers are fixed first. Because every run replaces its own day, running it again after a partial failure is harmless.
steps.code: airflow backfill create --dag-id daily_totals \ --from-date 2026-08-09 --to-date 2026-11-06 \ --reprocess-behavior completed --max-active-runs 8 --run-backwards

lab.title: A DAG runner with retries and backfills, on virtual time
steps: Run the tests. All 13 fail on TODOs. Read Warehouse.kt and PaymentTasks.kt first: the pipeline is extract (5 minutes), load (10) and report (5), and Faults makes chosen attempts crash right after their writes.

Exercise 1, Dag.topologicalOrder: Kahn's algorithm. Count each task's unfinished dependencies, keep the ready tasks in id order, and throw IllegalArgumentException if some tasks never become ready (a cycle).

Exercise 2, DagRunner.run: run the tasks in that order on a clock that starts at startMinute. A task whose dependencies didn't all succeed is UPSTREAM_FAILED and never runs. Each attempt adds the task's minutes; a failed attempt waits retryDelayMinutes and tries again, up to maxRetries retries.
Exercise 3, DagRunner.backfill: maxActiveRuns slots, each day given to the slot that is free earliest. The timing test expects 23 waves of 20 minutes for 90 days at 4 runs at a time.

Exercise 4, overwriteDailyTotal: the idempotent load. Then look at what the append test proves about the given appendDailyTotal, and at the test where latestDailyTotal copies today into every backfilled day.
Run until all 13 pass. The last one is a jqwik property: 30 random crash patterns, and your overwrite load must match the source every time.
hints: Kahn: waiting = tasks.associate { it.id to it.deps.size }, dependents grouped by dependency, ready = sortedSetOf<String>(). Take ready.first(), append it, decrement its dependents, add those that reach 0. If the order is shorter than the task list, there's a cycle.

In run, wrap the action: runCatching { task.action(RunContext(logicalDate, attempt, warehouse)) }.isSuccess. The first attempt plus maxRetries retries means attempt > maxRetries is the last one. Record attempts per task, 0 for a task that never ran.
In backfill, val freeAt = LongArray(maxActiveRuns); for each day val slot = freeAt.indices.minBy { freeAt[it] }, run with startMinute = freeAt[slot], then set freeAt[slot] to the run's end.
The idempotent load is one line different from the given append: ctx.warehouse.overwrite("daily_totals", ctx.logicalDate, listOf(total)).

drill.title: Make a nightly task safe to retry
drill.prompt: This task runs every night and is retried on failure: INSERT INTO fee_totals SELECT merchant_id, sum(fee_cents) FROM settlement_lines WHERE settled_at >= now() - INTERVAL '1 day' GROUP BY merchant_id. From memory, name its two problems and rewrite it so that a retry, or a backfill of any past day, leaves the right numbers. Use :day for the run's logical date.

answer.html: -- problem 1: now() makes the input depend on when the task runs, so a retry or a backfill reads another window -- problem 2: INSERT INTO adds a second copy of every merchant's total on each retry BEGIN; DELETE FROM fee_totals WHERE day = :day; -- replace the day, never add to it INSERT INTO fee_totals (day, merchant_id, fee_cents) SELECT :day, merchant_id, sum(fee_cents) FROM settlement_lines WHERE settled_at >= :day AND settled_at < :day + INTERVAL '1 day' -- the logical date's input only GROUP BY merchant_id; COMMIT;

recap: Three layers schedule batch work: the workflow orchestrator (Airflow, Dagster, Prefect) decides when each job runs, in what order and for which logical date; the engine (the Spark driver) schedules and retries a job's tasks; the resource manager (Kubernetes, YARN) places processes on machines.
A DAG states dependencies, so a job starts when its inputs are complete instead of at a guessed time, and every run is for one logical date.

Retries happen at every layer, so tasks must be idempotent: read the logical date's partition (never the latest data or now()), replace that date's output in one commit, and keep outside effects in their own task with a record of what was done.

Speculative execution copies a straggling task to another machine, which fixes a slow machine and does nothing for skew. Spark leaves it off by default because both copies run, so outputs must commit atomically.

A backfill runs the DAG for past dates. Cap it with --max-active-runs (backfill tasks aren't deprioritized), size it in waves, run it backwards to get recent days first, and expect --reprocess-behavior completed to rerun days that already succeeded.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why your settlement totals were 28% too high after a quarter of nightly runs that all showed green, and what you changed so that retries and backfills are safe.
explain.answer: Every run showed green because every task eventually succeeded, but some of them succeeded on their second or third attempt. The load task appended the day's total with INSERT INTO. On some nights its worker died after the insert had committed but before it told the orchestrator it was done, so the orchestrator treated the attempt as failed and ran it again, and the retry inserted the same total a second time. Nights that crashed twice were counted three times. Nothing failed, so nothing alerted; the numbers just drifted up. Retries didn't cause the problem, they exposed that the task wasn't idempotent. We changed the task in two ways. It now reads only the partition for its logical date, never the latest data or the current time, so any rerun of 6 November sees the same input. And it replaces that day's output in one transaction (delete the day and insert it, or overwrite the partition) instead of appending, so a second attempt leaves exactly what the first one did. With that, retries are safe, and we could backfill the whole quarter with reprocess set to completed to repair the history, newest days first, with a cap on concurrent runs so the nightly jobs kept running.

deeper.html:
Resource managers deserve a closer look if you run your own clusters. YARN splits the work into a central ResourceManager, a NodeManager on every machine, and one ApplicationMaster per job that negotiates for containers; Kubernetes has its scheduler, a kubelet per node, and operators that play the ApplicationMaster's role. Both keep their state in a coordination service (ZooKeeper for YARN's high availability, etcd for Kubernetes), which the Consistency and consensus track covers. Spark executors and machine learning jobs want all their containers at once or none, since half the executors can deadlock waiting for the other half. The default Kubernetes scheduler places pods one at a time, which is why Spark's documentation names batch schedulers such as Volcano and Apache YuniKorn.

Preemption changes how you size jobs. Tasks on spot or preemptible capacity are cheap and get killed, so you want many small tasks (the MapReduce paper ran 200,000 map tasks on 2,000 machines) and outputs that survive a lost executor. Spark's graceful decommissioning (spark.decommission.enabled) moves shuffle and cached blocks off an executor that is about to be removed, and remote shuffle services keep shuffle data outside the executors entirely.

Orchestrators keep growing toward data. Airflow 3 added DAG versioning, so a run finishes on the code it started with, and event-driven scheduling on top of assets. Dagster's partitioned assets make "which days of this table are stale?" a question the orchestrator can answer. Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition) covers job orchestration, preemption and workflows in chapter 11.
